Osteomyelitis

A small sham-controlled pilot found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated foot ulcers, and a very small jaw study found better postoperative healing and pain relief. Neither establishes eradication of bone infection.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small sham-controlled pilot found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated foot ulcers, and a very small jaw study found better postoperative healing and pain relief. Neither establishes eradication of bone infection.

Summary of the Evidence

Four unique publications were identified: one sham-controlled randomized pilot in people with osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers, one small controlled nonrandomized jaw study, one two-patient foot-ulcer case series combining PBM with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), and one rat MRSA osteomyelitis experiment. The diabetic-foot reports are narrowly mapped from a wound category: the randomized trial measured ulcer closure, not eradication of bone infection, while the case series cannot separate PBM from PRP. No duplicate cohort was identified among these four publications.

Human and clinical evidence

In the sham-controlled pilot, 20 people with severe diabetic foot ulcers described as osteomyelitis-associated received standard care plus active or sham at-home PBM. Seven of ten active-treatment participants achieved more than 90% wound closure, compared with one of ten in the sham group. Wound-size reduction also favored PBM. These results concern closure of the associated ulcer; the trial did not establish microbiological or radiological clearance of osteomyelitis (Haze et al. 2022).

A prospective controlled study of eight people with secondary chronic osteomyelitis of the jaws compared standard postoperative care with or without PBM. The four treated patients had better clinical-achievement scores at three and six months, and pain and discomfort resolved more often. The groups were very small and allocation was not randomized (Keković et al. 2023).

A two-case series of chronic diabetic-foot ulcers with osteomyelitis reported smaller wounds, healthier granulation tissue, and less necrotic tissue after a combined laser and PRP approach. Because both modalities and standard wound care were used together, these cases cannot identify the effect of PBM alone (Sani and Sani 2025).

Animal evidence

In a rat chronic osteomyelitis model caused by MRSA, debridement plus 808-nm near-infrared laser treatment was associated with dose-related reductions in histopathological infection compared with untreated controls. The experiment supports an antimicrobial or tissue-level effect in that specific model, not a clinical bone-infection cure (Kaya et al. 2011).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell-culture or ex-vivo study directly testing PBM for osteomyelitis was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The diabetic-foot pilot used daily pulsed 808-nm near-infrared light at 8.8 J/cm², applied directly to the wound at home for up to 12 weeks. The jaw study used an extraoral pulsed 635-nm red LED at 2.5 Hz for five sessions over two weeks. The rat study compared 808-nm near-infrared exposures of 7.64, 15.29, and 22.93 J/cm² after debridement. The routes, doses, and outcomes differ, and no common clinical dose has been established.

Interpretation

One small randomized pilot reported substantially greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers, and the jaw study reported better postoperative healing and pain outcomes. The rat experiment found dose-related improvement in infection histology. Human studies have not yet shown that PBM clears bone infection or prevents recurrence, so wound closure and pain should not be presented as infection eradication.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term wound closure in osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers Low for postoperative jaw healing and pain Very low for bone infection eradication
Publications and records4 relevant publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A small sham-controlled trial found greater closure of osteomyelitis-associated diabetic foot ulcers, while a four-versus-four jaw study found better clinical healing and pain outcomes after surgery. These results do not establish bone-infection eradication, and a two-case foot series combined PBM with platelet-rich plasma. Independent trials should include bone-infection outcomes and recurrence.
